He chases at 34.3%, which is the real concern: if pitchers solve him with stuff he can't lay off, the contact numbers erode before the power does. reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact profile and the chase rate are pointing in opposite directions, and that gap defines Walker. His 92.4 mph average exit velocity and 13.5% barrel rate sit comfortably in the top tier of the league, and the .484 xSLG backs up what that contact quality suggests about his power ceiling. But a 35.6% chase rate and 30.7% whiff rate are genuine holes that pitchers will keep attacking until he adjusts, which is why a hitter this loud at contact is still carrying a 24.3% strikeout rate. If he tightens the zone enough to let that exit velocity breathe across a full season, you're looking at a .282/.341/.492 line with 31 home runs and 21 steals in 672 plate appearances, a genuine middle-of-the-order corner outfielder. If he doesn't, pitchers keep expanding and the power plays in bursts rather than as a season-long force.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The contact profile is almost separable from the strikeout number, and that's the whole tension here. At the plate, a .404 xwOBA and 16.3% barrel rate say elite hitter; a 30.8% whiff rate says a pitch he can't catch up to still exists, but the 13.4% walk rate keeps him on base even when he's fooled, and the projection's .384 OBP across 693 PA reflects exactly that. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate against hitters describe a front-line starter, and the 98.1 mph fastball at 2488 rpm explains how the whiffs are generated without needing to chase a lot of weak contact out of the zone. The one variable the profile can't answer yet is whether the elbow holds across a full two-way workload in Los Angeles: if it does, a projected .929 OPS and ace-caliber pitching in the same uniform is what you get; if the pitching side is managed conservatively, you still have one of the most dangerous bats in any order.

At 12.8% BB%, Busch sits in the 90th percentile, and that discipline is doing the work his raw contact numbers can't — his xBA sits at .232 and his average exit velocity at 88.3 mph, neither of which screams impact bat. What he actually is: a first baseman who earns his way on base, barrels enough balls (9.2%) to project 21 home runs across a full season, and runs an .OBP of .352 that keeps him from being a liability in a lineup. The whole thing hinges on whether pitchers eventually exploit the contact vulnerability at a higher clip, because if the strikeout rate climbs past that 23.0%, the walk rate alone won't be enough to carry a .754 OPS at a corner spot. A solid second-division regular is the honest ceiling here, and he's already living it.

reports.name: Logan Gilbert
reports.published_report: The contact quality numbers are the thing to sit with: a 10.0% barrel rate and 41.5% hard-hit rate that both land in the bottom quarter of the league, yet he posts a 3.70 xERA and .298 xwOBA that say solid mid-rotation starter, not punching-bag. The reconciliation is the walk rate. At 6.3% he's in the 84th percentile, and his 29.7% whiff rate does enough damage that he doesn't need to be a barrel-suppressor to get through lineups. The projection covers 187.1 innings with a 3.41 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, and 196 strikeouts; that's the version of Gilbert where the command holds and the contact he does allow stays manageable, but if the barrel rate creeps north and the zone control slips even modestly, the 3.70 xERA is already showing you the ceiling of the good outcome. A durable, reliable number-two type who lives or dies by the precision of his attack.

reports.name: Brandon Marsh

reports.name: Chandler Simpson
reports.published_report: The contact-and-speed profile here is about as pure as it gets, and the Statcast card makes clear exactly what that means. His 8.3% strikeout rate sits at the 99th percentile, and his 10.3% whiff rate matches it — he's making contact at an elite clip, full stop. The problem lives on the other end: an 83.8 mph average exit velocity and 13.2% hard-hit rate, both at the 1st percentile, and an xSLG of .294 that tells you the contact itself carries almost no damage. He profiles as a .305/.335/.360 hitter across 599 plate appearances, reaching base on weak grounders and legging out hits, stealing 42 bases, and contributing almost nothing over the fence, with value entirely downstream of his 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and the batting average it inflates. If the speed erodes, the .263 xwOBA is what remains, and that's a bench bat at best.

reports.name: Brooks Lee
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost uniformly grim: .273 xwOBA at the 3rd percentile, xBA of .223, a 6.4% walk rate that sits well below average. And yet the projection still has him hitting 24 home runs across a full season. If the raw power ever catches up to what the chase behavior costs him, he's a useful right-side-of-the-infield piece who banks on volume; if it doesn't, .247/.299 with modest over-the-fence production is the ceiling, not the floor.

Miles gets hitters out by keeping the ball on the ground and off the barrel, a 3.8% barrel rate in the 94th percentile and average exit velocity sitting at 86.8 mph, rather than by missing bats, and his 18.3% whiff rate in the 5th percentile makes that explicit. The 6.0% walk rate is clean, and when hitters do put the ball in play they're not squaring it up, which is how you post results that look like a mid-bullpen strikeout artist without actually being one. If his contact management regresses and the chase rate, already at 28.5%, dips further, there's no swing-and-miss floor to catch him, so the profile lives and dies on weak contact, and with 92.7 projected innings and a 3.03 ERA he's priced as a legitimate bullpen contributor for Toronto whose Statcast contact suppression says the number is earned.

reports.name: Roki Sasaki
reports.published_report:
The fastball at 97.8 mph is elite. The problem is what happens after it.

Sasaki's 29.7% whiff rate and 33.4% chase rate say he misses bats at a real clip, but the barrel and hard-hit numbers tell a different story: hitters who do make contact are doing damage, with a 10.0% barrel rate and 43.1% hard-hit rate that land in the bottom tier of the league. The xERA sits at 4.40 and the projection matches it almost exactly at 4.55, which means the stuff-to-results gap that scouts hoped would close in MLB hasn't closed yet. If the command tightens, that 9.4% walk rate is the number this profile hinges on, and he becomes a genuine mid-rotation arm with a plus fastball doing real work. If it doesn't, a bloated WHIP and loud contact are the outcome, not a stepping stone.

reports.name: Bryan Reynolds
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here. At 13.1%, Reynolds draws free passes at a rate that puts him in elite company for the position, and that discipline is why the .365 OBP holds even when the .249 xBA says he's a perfectly average contact maker. The 46.4% hard-hit rate and .350 xwOBA confirm the power plays — the gap between his xSLG and his projection's .423 SLG is narrow enough to trust. What keeps this profile from being truly premium is the 28.9% whiff rate, which drags against all that plate patience and caps the ceiling at a solid everyday outfielder rather than anything more; if pitchers ever learn to exploit that contact vulnerability more aggressively, the walk rate and the production follow each other down together.

reports.name: Brandon Lowe
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the power metrics tell completely different stories, and the 32 projected home runs are only believable if you start with the power side. At 91.1 mph average exit velocity with an 11.9% barrel rate and 46.0% hard-hit rate, the bat genuinely gets to loud contact, and that .424 xSLG reflects a real quality-of-contact profile. The problem is a 35.2% whiff rate sitting at the 4th percentile, paired with a 33.7% chase rate, which is how a hitter posts a .235 xBA while also posting a .321 xwOBA: he hits the ball hard when he hits it, and misses a lot. The projection's .247/.315/.464 line holds if you believe the hard contact keeps outrunning the strikeouts, and the barrel rate gives you reasonable cause to think it can, but if the whiff rate climbs further or the barrel rate dips, the batting average gets ugly fast and the power number shrinks with it.

reports.name: James Triantos

Twenty-five stolen bases add a real dimension, but if the gap power doesn't develop beyond what he's shown, you're looking at a bench bat whose entire value lives inside a contact rate that has to hold in a harder environment.

report_llm.text: The walk rate is the whole argument, and it's also the whole problem. Xavier Neyens has drawn 109 walks across A+ & A this season, a 25% BB rate that translates to 16.4% at the MLB level, against a big-league average of 8.5%. The trouble is that same 430-PA line carries a 33% strikeout rate, and the MLB translation pushes that to 36.2%, while the ISO fades from .206 in the minors to .135 in translation, a tick below what a typical major leaguer produces. If the contact quality firms up as he ages into his strength, the .435 OBP profile is the seed of a legitimate everyday corner; if the strikeouts don't bend, the walk rate alone leaves him a patient, low-average hitter who never quite hits enough to hold a lineup spot.

reports.name: Liomar Martinez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is electric and the walk rate is a problem, both true at once, and that tension is the whole profile. Across 95.3 innings at A+, Martinez has struck out 139 batters at 13.1 K/9, sitting at the 94th percentile among his peers, while issuing 56 walks at 5.3 BB/9, sitting at the 37th. Run those through an MLB-equivalent lens and the strikeouts translate to 9.3 per nine, but the walks translate to the same 5.3, leaving a K-BB% of 12.7% against a pool where the average is 13.5%. The ceiling here lives or dies on whether he can find the strike zone with enough consistency to let the swing-and-miss play; if it holds, there's a backend arm buried in there, and if it doesn't, the walks swallow the strikeouts and you're left with a depth arm who misses bats but can't stay in lineups.
reports.report: The stuff is ahead of the strike throwing right now; the bat-missing is starter-caliber. Keep the starter path open, but the walk rate has to move before the bullpen risk fades. The sample covers 95.3 IP in High-A, so confidence is low.

reports.name: Walbert Ureña
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 97.8 mph, which is legitimate leverage, but a 12.8% walk rate is quietly the whole argument here. Contact suppression is genuine: a 5.1% barrel rate, 34.2% hard-hit rate, and .288 xwOBA all point to a pitcher who limits damage when hitters make contact, and the 27.1% whiff rate suggests the stuff plays beyond raw velocity. But 12.8% free passes is a rate that unravels outings before the damage metrics even get a chance to matter, and at 22 the command floor is still being established. If he tightens the zone enough to let that contact profile breathe, a 3.44 xERA translates to a legitimate mid-rotation contributor; if the walks hold at current levels, he's a high-leverage arm waiting to be moved to shorter stints where the command cost is less punishing.

reports.name: Kyle Leahy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile and the projection are telling completely different stories, and the projection is the one worth questioning. A 4.84 xERA paired with a 48.0% hard-hit rate, that 1st-percentile contact-quality mark, don't resolve into a 3.31 ERA over time; they resolve into a pitcher who is getting squared up and surviving on something that won't hold. The walk rate is genuinely fine at 7.0%, and the projection credits him with 152.6 innings, but the underlying contact metrics say hitters are doing real damage when they connect. If strand rate normalizes or the defense cools off, the real Leahy looks a lot more like that 4.84 xERA than whatever the projection line is currently pricing in.

reports.name: Sal Frelick
reports.published_report: A 10.2% strikeout rate and an 11.2% whiff rate that both grade near the top of the league tell you exactly what Frelick is: a bat-to-ball specialist who makes consistent, clean contact. The problem is the contact doesn't go anywhere — 85.9 mph average exit velocity and a 2.4% barrel rate leave him with an xwOBA of .281, which is among the softest outcomes in the sport for a full-time outfielder. His 28.6 ft/s sprint speed and an ability to chase at just 24.0% keep him relevant, but unless the quality underneath the contact improves, the projection's .653 OPS is probably the ceiling, not the floor.

Alderman's 33 K% at AAA translates to 30.7% in MLB-equivalent terms, and his walk rate converts to just 8.2%, essentially what a league-average hitter produces — meaning there's no patience floor propping him up when the swing-and-miss follows him north. reports.name: Mason Fluharty
reports.published_report: The xERA of 2.78 and a 35.4% chase rate tell the same story: hitters aren't squaring him up, and when they chase, they're not doing damage. Fluharty's contact suppression is the engine — a 31.7% hard-hit rate and 86.3 mph average exit velocity both sit in the 90th percentile or better, which is why the xwOBA of .260 holds even without a dominant strikeout rate. The walk rate at 10.2% is the load-bearing problem; it's the reason the projection ERA (3.59) drifts well above the xERA, and it's the reason the ceiling here is a setup-caliber arm rather than a closer. If he brings the walks down, the contact profile makes him genuinely difficult to score on; if he doesn't, he's a middle reliever propped up by batted-ball luck he's actually earned.

His xBA sits at .246 while his xSLG is .449, which means the bat is generating real damage on contact but not finding enough grass, and a .238 projection is an honest translation of that pattern. The 91.0 mph average exit velocity and 46.8% hard-hit rate say the power hasn't aged out; the projection's 18 home runs across 456 PA reflects a hitter who still lifts and drives the ball but whose counting-stat floor is capped by a shrinking role. If the PA total climbs closer to a full season's worth, the power profile supports more than 18; if it doesn't, he's a productive mid-lineup piece playing fewer games than you'd want from him.

reports.name: Owen Carey
reports.published_report: The ISO is the best thing in the profile. Across AA & A+, a .195 ISO at 19 years old is loud, and the translation holds it at .142 at the MLB level — below-average power once the level discount applies, which is the whole tension here. The contact and walk rates read fine in the minors, but the MLB translation puts his K% at 23.1 and his BB% at 7.5, both nudging the wrong side of average, leaving a profile that lives and dies on whether the raw power scales faster than those discipline numbers flatten out. If the bat speed and loft play up as he matures, he becomes a fringy everyday corner outfielder; if the strikeouts creep and the power doesn't translate, the floor is organizational depth, and that ceiling isn't far enough above the floor to feel comfortable at 19.

reports.name: Dante Nori
reports.published_report: Thirteen stolen bases in 261 plate appearances across three levels is the loudest thing on this card, and it may also be the only thing that survives a translation to the big leagues. The MLB-equivalent ISO sits at .116, well short of the .150 league average, and the walk rate translates to 7.3% when the typical big leaguer draws at 8.5%. Neither number suggests a bat that will carry its own weight in a lineup. What keeps this profile alive is whether the speed plays in center at the highest level and whether the contact, a .243 average across AA & A+ & A, ticks up enough to make the on-base number functional; if it does, you have a bench option with real value on the bases, and if it doesn't, you have a depth piece who is fast but doesn't get on base enough for that speed to matter.

report_llm.text: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that makes you squint. Farmelo has drawn 86 walks across AA & A+ in 2026, a 16% clip that translates to 11.9% at the MLB level, meaningful separation from where most big-league hitters land, but the strikeout picture darkens that considerably: 143 punchouts at a 26% rate that translates to 29.2%, roughly seven points above what MLB pitching typically extracts. The .184 ISO and 37 stolen bases across AA & A+ give him a real tool set to work with, but if the strikeout rate doesn't come down as pitching sharpens, the power translates to .134 at the MLB level, and the on-base gains from the walks get eaten away quickly. The floor here is a bench piece who runs and takes pitches; the ceiling doesn't clear that by much unless the contact quality improves in a meaningful way.

reports.name: Emmet Sheehan
reports.published_report:
The strikeout-to-contact tension is the whole profile. Sheehan generates whiffs on 30.8% of swings and gets chased at 35.0%, yet hitters are barreling him at 10.5%, which sits in the bottom tenth of the league.

The xERA of 3.97 says the underlying skill holds when he's missing bats, and a 26.2% strikeout rate is a legitimate weapon. The problem is that when contact does land, it lands hard, and the 5.16 ERA projection reflects how costly those mistakes become across 102.8 innings.

If he limits the damage in the zone, there's a mid-rotation floor here. If barrel rate stays where it is, he's a rotation filler burning through run support.

reports.name: Jared Dickey
reports.published_report: The contact skills are genuine, the power is not. Across AAA & AA in 2026, Dickey has drawn 54 walks against just 69 strikeouts in 421 plate appearances, and that discipline translates to a MLB-equivalent walk rate of 10.7% where the league average sits at 8.5%, with a strikeout rate well below average at 19.2%. The problem is the .135 ISO, which comes out to roughly .120 at the MLB level where the typical hitter lands at .150, and right field without impact power is a profile that shrinks fast. If he sticks and the gap power comes, he's a low-end regular; if it doesn't, the bat-to-ball and patience make him a useful bench piece who earns a roster spot but not a lineup spot.

The power is where the ceiling caps: a .153 ISO across AAA & AA translates to .13 at the MLB level, right at the 0.15 MLB average, and a 6% walk rate across AAA & AA translates to 6.4%, a shade below the 8.5% MLB baseline. Joshua Kuroda-Grauer is a near-term bench or platoon bat if the contact holds, and a fringe depth piece if pitchers neutralize what is right now a genuinely elite skill — the 15 stolen bases alongside that bat control keep the floor from being empty, but it's narrow.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

The walk rate is the one honest wrinkle: 15 free passes in 29 AAA innings translates to 3.8 per nine in the majors, a little loose for a rotation piece, and that's what the floor hinges on. If the IL stint is short and the command firms up, he's more than a depth arm; if the walks don't tighten, that depth ceiling is probably where he lands.

reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.

reports.name: Drew Cavanaugh
reports.published_report: The .449 OBP across AAA & AA is doing a lot of work here, and the BABIP of .401 is doing most of the heavy lifting behind it. Cavanaugh has 35 walks against 55 strikeouts in 227 plate appearances, which translates to an 11.4% walk rate when moved to an MLB context, comfortably above the 8.5% MLB baseline. The MLB-equivalent ISO comes out to .170, just nudging past that same baseline figure of .150, which is fine for a catcher but not the kind of carrying tool that survives a BABIP correction. If the average regresses hard and the power stays modest, you're left with a patient backstop who can work counts at the margin, which is a bench catcher, not a regular.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

The whole read hinges on whether he can find the zone more consistently as he works through AA, because right now the stuff isn't missing enough bats to survive the walks.

reports.name: Jack Hurley
reports.published_report: The translation is the problem. Across AAA & AA in 204 plate appearances, Hurley is hitting .254/.332/.409, which looks passable until you run it through the MLB equivalent and find a strikeout rate of 25.5% where the league sits at 22.0, paired with a translated ISO of .135 where the league average lands at .150. The contact-and-power combo that would need to work together doesn't clear the bar at either end. If the hit tool sharpens and the strikeout rate drops, there's a low-end regular hiding in a left field profile; if it doesn't, 15 walks in 204 plate appearances across AAA & AA is the whole argument, and that's a bench bat at best.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.

reports.name: Mccade Brown
reports.published_report: The K-BB% is the loudest thing in this profile, ranking 97th among pitchers in his pool at AA, and the 43 innings he threw before the shoulder shut him down show a 3.1 ERA and 1.1 WHIP that hold up against that control picture. Across AA & A+, the translated strikeout rate lands at 9.2 per nine while the MLB average sits at 8.6, and the walk rate comes back at 3.7 against a league figure of 3.2, which is the one honest friction in an otherwise clean command profile. If the right shoulder heals clean and the control holds in translation, he's a functional big-league reliever; if the shoulder costs him anything on the stuff side, the walk rate has nowhere to hide and you're left with a depth arm on a thin margin.

reports.name: Wilson Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The walk rate is loud for a 21-year-old at A+: 58 walks across 364 plate appearances, with a translated BB% of 11.4 against a big-league pool that averages 8.5. That's the selling point. The power doesn't come with it — an ISO of .167 at A+ translates to .127 in the majors, meaningfully short of the 8.5 average, and the 20 stolen bases show he knows he has to manufacture something when he does get on. If the plate discipline holds as he climbs and the raw pop develops enough to punish pitchers for nibbling, there's a fringe regular in here; if the power stays where it is, he's a bench piece with a useful OBP, and the ceiling note in the data says the system agrees.
